etymology: From the Hebrew mo’zney mirmah, “balances of deceit,” the dishonest scales weighted to cheat, set against the even shelemah, the “just weight” that is the LORD’s delight.
biblical_def: A false balance is the rigged scale of the dishonest tradesman, weighted to defraud the buyer or the seller, and the Scripture declares plainly that it is an abomination to the LORD, while a just weight is His delight (Pro 11:1). The matter is no small one in the eyes of God, for He repeats it: divers weights and divers measures, both of them are alike abomination to the LORD (Pro 20:23). The prophets thundered against the men of commerce who made the ephah small and the shekel great, and falsified the balances by deceit, that they might buy the poor for silver and the needy for a pair of shoes (Amo 8:5). Micah asks whether God can count the wicked pure with the scant measure and the bag of deceitful weights (Mic 6:11). The false balance is therefore a figure of every dishonesty that wears the look of fairness while the hand secretly tips the scale. The LORD who weigheth the spirits is Himself the true balance, and He will not hold guiltless the man who weigheth out injustice under the show of trade. The dictionary marks that a just weight is more than a rule of the market; it is a confession that the God of truth sees the secret thumb upon the scale, and that He delights in the upright dealing that fears Him in the hidden things.
webster_summary: A dishonest weight or scale, weighted to defraud, declared an abomination to the LORD.
webster_full: FALSE BALANCE, a deceitful scale or weight, used to cheat in buying and selling.
It stands opposed to the just weight, which is called the LORD’s delight.
The Scripture names divers weights and divers measures alike an abomination to God.
The prophets condemned the merchants who falsified the balances by deceit.
It witnesses to the LORD’s care for honesty in the hidden dealings of men.
scriptures: Pro 11:1
A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight.
Divers weights are an abomination unto the LORD; and a false balance is not good.
Amo 8:5
Saying, When will the new moon be gone, that we may sell corn? and the sabbath, that we may set forth wheat, making the ephah small, and the shekel great, and falsifying the balances by deceit?
Mic 6:11
Shall I count them pure with the wicked balances, and with the bag of deceitful weights?
corruption_summary: The false balance is now wielded against truth itself, in the relativizing of every weight and measure by situational ethics.
corruption_paragraphs: Beyond the marketplace, the false balance has become a figure of the present age’s dealing with truth. Where Scripture sets one fixed and righteous standard, the spirit of the times keeps a bag of deceitful weights, measuring the same deed light in a friend and heavy in a foe, calling the same word good today and evil tomorrow. This is the false balance of situational ethics, which weighs every act not against the unchanging law of God but against the shifting advantage of the hour, and so makes the ephah small and the shekel great as it pleases.

The dictionary answers that the LORD is no respecter of persons and keeps no divers weights. His balance is just, His measure full, His word the same yesterday, today, and for ever. To judge by a moving standard is to falsify the balances by deceit, and the God who weigheth the spirits will not count pure the man who carries two measures in his bag. The recovery is a fixed weight of truth, the upright dealing of those who fear God in the secret things, and the confession that a just weight, in commerce and in judgment alike, is His delight.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for “balances of deceit,” the false balance names the rigged scale the LORD abhors.
roots_lines: False Balance — Hebrew mo’zney mirmah, “balances of deceit.”
It stands against the even shelemah, the “just” or “perfect weight.”
Solomon names it an abomination to the LORD in the Proverbs.
Amos and Micah condemn the merchants who falsify the balances.
The LORD who weigheth the spirits is Himself the true balance.
usage: Like the false balance the LORD abhors, every double standard of judgment is an abomination before the God of truth.
The believer who fears God carries one weight in his bag, dealing uprightly in the hidden things no man sees.
A just weight is the LORD’s delight, in the market and in the judgment of our brother alike.

etymology: From the Hebrew tsa‘aq and za‘aq, “to cry out, to cry for help,” and the Greek boæ, “a crying,” the loud appeal of the afflicted believer unto God.
biblical_def: The cry of the saint is the believer’s loud and earnest appeal unto God in his affliction, and the sure word of Scripture is that the LORD hears it. The righteous cry, and the LORD heareth, and delivereth them out of all their troubles (Psa 34:17). It is no genteel or measured thing, this cry; Heman the Ezrahite poured it out in the night season, crying day and night before God when his soul was full of troubles and his life drew nigh unto the grave (Psa 88:1-2). The Lord Jesus taught that God will avenge His own elect, which cry day and night unto Him, though He bear long with them (Luk 18:7). And under the altar the souls of the martyrs cry with a loud voice, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood (Rev 6:10). The dictionary marks that this crying is the proper voice of faith in distress, not unbelief, for the man who cries unto God still believes that God hears and will answer. The saint may cry from the depths, from the pit, from the place where no comfort comes, and yet his cry is heard in heaven and laid up before the throne. The crying of the saint is therefore a comfort and not a shame, for it leads at last to the wiping away of every tear by the hand of God Himself.
webster_summary: The earnest appeal of the afflicted believer unto God, which the LORD surely hears.
webster_full: CRY OF THE SAINT, the loud and earnest appeal of the afflicted believer unto God.
The psalmist promises that the LORD heareth the cry of the righteous.
It is poured out in the night season from the depths of trouble.
Christ taught that God avengeth His elect who cry day and night unto Him.
It witnesses to the faith that cries because it believes God hears and answers.
scriptures: The righteous cry, and the LORD heareth, and delivereth them out of all their troubles.
Psa 88:1
O LORD God of my salvation, I have cried day and night before thee:
Luk 18:7
And shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him, though he bear long with them?
Rev 6:10
And they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?
corruption_summary: A scriptural mark of true faith, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses to the LORD’s sure hearing of His afflicted people.
corruption_paragraphs: The cry of the saint is a plain and precious truth of Scripture, and no movement of the present age has set itself to redefine it. The dictionary records it that the believer who is brought low and cries from the depths may know his crying is no token of unbelief, but the proper voice of faith laying hold upon a God who hears.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the boldness of the afflicted believer at the throne of grace. He who heard Heman in the night and hears the martyrs under the altar is the same who bids His people cast their care upon Him. The saint tempted to think God deaf to his groaning may remember that the righteous cry and the LORD heareth, and that not one cry of His people falls unregarded to the ground.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew and Greek for “to cry out,” the cry of the saint names the believer’s appeal that God surely hears.
roots_lines: Cry of the Saint — Hebrew tsa‘aq, “to cry for help.”
The Greek boæ names “a crying” or loud appeal.
The psalmist Heman cried day and night before God in his trouble.
Christ named the elect as those who cry day and night unto Him.
The souls under the altar cry with a loud voice for the LORD’s judgment.
usage: Like the cry of the saint that the LORD heareth, the believer’s groaning in affliction is the proper voice of faith, not of unbelief.
When the soul is brought to the pit, the cry that ascends from the depths is heard and laid up before the throne of God.
The God who avengeth His own elect bids His afflicted people cry day and night, assured that He will answer in His time.

etymology: From the Hebrew idiom mille’ acharey, literally “to fill up after” the LORD, to follow Him fully and without reserve, the word spoken of Caleb who had another spirit with him.
biblical_def: To wholly follow the LORD is to follow Him fully, with the whole heart, holding nothing back, and it is the word the Scripture sets as a crown upon Caleb the son of Jephunneh. When ten spies brought an evil report and the people murmured, the LORD said of Caleb that he had another spirit with him, and hath followed me fully, and him will I bring into the land whereinto he went (Num 14:24). Moses repeated it: none of that generation should see the good land save Caleb and Joshua, for they have wholly followed the LORD (Num 32:12; Deu 1:36). And Caleb himself, an old man of fourscore and five years, pleaded the promise, saying, I wholly followed the LORD my God (Jos 14:8-9). The Hebrew is a vivid one, to fill up after the LORD, to leave no empty place between the soul and its God, no part withheld, no reserve kept back for self. The dictionary marks that this is the very pattern of a true and persevering faith, not a fitful or half-hearted obedience, but a whole-souled cleaving to the LORD against the fear of giants and the murmuring of the multitude. To wholly follow is the mark of the elect, who endure to the end; and the great Captain of our salvation Himself wholly followed His Father’s will, even unto the death of the cross, that He might bring His people into the rest that remaineth.
webster_summary: To follow the LORD fully and without reserve, as Caleb did, with another spirit.
webster_full: WHOLLY FOLLOW, to follow the LORD fully, with the whole heart, holding nothing back.
The Hebrew idiom means “to fill up after” the LORD, leaving no reserve.
It is the word spoken of Caleb, who had another spirit with him.
Caleb and Joshua alone of their generation wholly followed and entered the land.
It witnesses to the whole-souled, persevering faith of the LORD’s elect.
scriptures: But my servant Caleb, because he had another spirit with him, and hath followed me fully, him will I bring into the land whereinto he went; and his seed shall possess it.
Save Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenezite, and Joshua the son of Nun: for they have wholly followed the LORD.
Deu 1:36
Save Caleb the son of Jephunneh; he shall see it, and to him will I give the land that he hath trodden upon, and to his children, because he hath wholly followed the LORD.
Jos 14:8
Nevertheless my brethren that went up with me made the heart of the people melt: but I wholly followed the LORD my God.
corruption_summary: A scriptural mark of true faith, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses to the whole-souled following the LORD requires.
corruption_paragraphs: To wholly follow the LORD is a plain commendation of Scripture, and no movement of the present age has troubled itself to redefine it. The dictionary records it that the believer may know the difference between a fitful, partial obedience and the whole-hearted cleaving to God that the LORD honoured in Caleb and will honour still.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the wholeness of true discipleship, which fills up after the LORD and keeps no part back for self. He who praised Caleb for following Him fully is the same who calls His people to love Him with all the heart, soul, mind, and strength. The saint content with a divided heart may remember Caleb, who at fourscore and five could plead that he had wholly followed the LORD, and who entered the inheritance for which the half-hearted fell in the wilderness.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew “to fill up after” the LORD, to wholly follow names the whole-souled cleaving of Caleb’s faith.
roots_lines: Wholly Follow — Hebrew mille’ acharey, “to fill up after.”
It means to follow the LORD fully, leaving no reserve.
The LORD said Caleb had another spirit and followed Him fully.
Caleb and Joshua alone of their generation entered the land.
Caleb pleaded the word in his old age, having wholly followed God.
usage: Like Caleb who wholly followed the LORD, the true believer fills up after his God, holding nothing back for self.
Against the murmuring of the multitude and the fear of giants, the elect cleave to the LORD with the whole heart.
The half-hearted fall in the wilderness, but the saint who wholly follows enters the rest that remaineth.

etymology: A descriptive phrase for the half-obedience the Scripture condemns; from the account of Saul, who chamal, “spared” or “had pity upon” what God had devoted to destruction.
biblical_def: Incomplete obedience is the half-keeping of God’s commandment that, because it withholds in part, is reckoned as disobedience altogether. The pattern is Saul at Amalek, who was bidden utterly to destroy all, but spared Agag the king and the best of the sheep and the oxen and the fatlings, and would not utterly destroy them; only the vile and refuse he destroyed (1Sa 15:9). When Samuel met him, Saul protested that he had performed the commandment of the LORD, but the lowing of the cattle and the bleating of the sheep gave the lie to his words. Then came the prophet’s great rebuke: Hath the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams. For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry (1Sa 15:22-23). The dictionary marks the solemn truth that to obey in part, choosing which of God’s words to keep, is not partial righteousness but full rebellion dressed in the garment of religion. Saul kept the spoil to sacrifice, and called his disobedience worship; but the LORD rejected him from being king. The lesson is that no man may amend the commandment of God by his own wisdom, and that the whole obedience of faith, not the selective obedience of self-will, is what the LORD requires of His own.
webster_summary: The half-keeping of God’s commandment that, withholding in part, is counted as full disobedience.
webster_full: INCOMPLETE OBEDIENCE, the half-keeping of a command which, withholding in part, is reckoned disobedience.
The pattern is Saul, who spared Agag and the best of the spoil at Amalek.
He called his disobedience an offering and said he had obeyed the LORD.
Samuel answered that to obey is better than sacrifice.
It witnesses that selective obedience is rebellion, as the sin of witchcraft.
scriptures: But Saul and the people spared Agag, and the best of the sheep, and of the oxen, and of the fatlings, and the lambs, and all that was good, and would not utterly destroy them: but every thing that was vile and refuse, that they destroyed utterly.
And Samuel said, Hath the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.
For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry. Because thou hast rejected the word of the LORD, he hath also rejected thee from being king.
Jam 2:10
For whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all.
corruption_summary: The age dresses its selective obedience as devotion, keeping back what God commanded to be wholly given up.
corruption_paragraphs: Saul’s sin is no relic of an old war, for the same incomplete obedience walks abroad in every age and in every heart. The professor who keeps the commandments he finds agreeable and quietly spares the Agag he was bidden to slay does precisely what Saul did, and like Saul he often calls the sparing by a better name. The age is full of men who will obey God in the easy thing and reserve the costly thing for themselves, then offer their partial keeping as though it were full devotion, making a sacrifice of what God commanded them to surrender.

The dictionary answers with Samuel’s word that to obey is better than sacrifice, and that to keep back any part of what God has devoted is rebellion, counted before Him as the sin of witchcraft. He who is guilty in one point is guilty of all. The recovery is the whole obedience of faith, which does not sit in judgment upon the commandment, choosing what to keep, but submits the whole man to the whole word of God, slaying the spared Agag of every cherished sin rather than leading it home alive.
roots_summary: From the account of Saul who spared what God devoted, incomplete obedience names the half-keeping that is full rebellion.
roots_lines: Incomplete Obedience — from Saul’s chamal, “he spared” or “pitied.”
Saul kept Agag and the best of the spoil against the LORD’s command.
He called the spared cattle an offering to the LORD.
Samuel declared that to obey is better than sacrifice.
Rebellion is named as the sin of witchcraft, and Saul was rejected.
usage: Like Saul who spared Agag, the heart that keeps God’s easy commands and reserves the costly one obeys in part and so disobeys altogether.
To call our disobedience an offering, as Saul called the spoil a sacrifice, is rebellion clothed in the garment of religion.
The believer is summoned to slay the spared Agag of every cherished sin, for to obey is better than sacrifice.

etymology: From the Greek chōra makra, “a distant region,” the place to which the prodigal son journeyed and wasted his substance with riotous living.
biblical_def: The far country is the distant land into which the younger son of the parable journeyed, when he had gathered all together and took his way from the father’s house, and there wasted his substance with riotous living (Luk 15:13). It is a place named not chiefly by its geography but by its distance from the father, a country far off from the home and the table and the embrace of love. There the prodigal spent all, and when a mighty famine arose in that land, he began to be in want (Luk 15:14). The dictionary marks that the far country is the very figure of the soul’s wandering from God, the self-chosen exile of the sinner who counts the father’s house a prison and liberty a thing to be found afar off. Its near approaches are fair, full of feasting and friends and the brief sweetness of sin; but its end is famine, want, and the swine’s field. The wonder of the parable is that the road into the far country is also the road home, for the same feet that carried the prodigal out carried him back when he came to himself and arose and went to his father. The far country thus preaches both the misery of departure from God and the riches of His grace, who runs to meet the returning sinner while he is yet a great way off, and falls on his neck, and kisses him.
webster_summary: The distant land to which the prodigal son journeyed and wasted his substance, a figure of the soul’s wandering from God.
webster_full: FAR COUNTRY, the distant land into which the prodigal son journeyed in the parable.
There he wasted his substance with riotous living and spent all.
It is named by its distance from the father’s house, not its place.
Its near pleasures end in famine, want, and the swine’s field.
It witnesses to the soul’s self-chosen exile from God, and the way home by grace.
scriptures: And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living.
And when he had spent all, there arose a mighty famine in that land; and he began to be in want.
Isa 53:6
All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.
Eph 2:13
But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ.
corruption_summary: A scriptural figure, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses to the soul’s wandering from God and the grace that brings it home.
corruption_paragraphs: The far country is a figure of our Lord’s own teaching, and no movement of the present age has troubled itself to redefine it. The dictionary records it that the reader may know the parable’s far country for what it is, the soul’s departure from the living God, and may trace in it both the misery of sin and the wonder of the Father’s welcome.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the true nature of sin as a wandering from the Father into want. He who pictured the prodigal in the far country is the same who runs to meet the returning sinner while he is yet a great way off. The saint who feels the famine of his own departures may remember that the road into the far country is also the road home, and that the Father waits with the best robe and the fatted calf for every son who comes to himself.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “a distant region,” the far country names the place of the prodigal’s wandering from the father.
roots_lines: Far Country — Greek chōra makra, “a distant region.”
It is the land into which the prodigal son journeyed.
There he wasted his substance with riotous living.
A mighty famine arose, and he began to be in want.
It figures the soul’s self-chosen exile far off from God.
usage: Like the prodigal in the far country, the wandering soul finds the feast of sin ends in famine and the swine’s field.
The far country is measured not in miles but in distance from the Father’s house and table.
The same road that carried the sinner out carries him home, where the Father runs to meet him a great way off.

etymology: From the Greek keratiōn, the “little horn,” the pods of the carob tree fed to swine, which the prodigal would fain have eaten in his want.
biblical_def: Husks are the pods of the carob, the coarse fodder of swine, and they name the lowest depth to which the prodigal sank in the far country, for he would fain have filled his belly with the husks that the swine did eat, and no man gave unto him (Luk 15:16). The picture is one of utter destitution: the son of a rich father, who had wasted his portion on riotous living, now so emptied of all that he envies the very swine their husks, and is denied even these. The dictionary marks that the husks are a figure of all that sin offers the soul when its first sweetness is spent. The world feeds its servants on husks, on that which is not bread and which satisfieth not, even as Isaiah cried, Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not? (Isa 55:2). The husk has a shape of nourishment but no substance of it; it fills the mouth and leaves the belly empty, and the soul that feeds on the provisions of sin rises ever hungry from the table. It was the famine of the husks that brought the prodigal to himself, when he remembered the bread enough and to spare in his father’s house. So the very emptiness of sin’s provision is made, by the mercy of God, a means to turn the wanderer home to the fulness that is in the Father.
webster_summary: The carob pods fed to swine, which the prodigal would have eaten in his want, a figure of sin’s empty provision.
webster_full: HUSKS, the pods of the carob tree, used as fodder for swine.
The prodigal would fain have filled his belly with them, and no man gave unto him.
They mark the lowest depth of his destitution in the far country.
They figure the empty provision of sin, which fills but does not satisfy.
It witnesses that the world feeds its servants on that which is not bread.
scriptures: And he would fain have filled his belly with the husks that the swine did eat: and no man gave unto him.
Isa 55:2

Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not? hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness.
Jer 2:13
For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.
Joh 6:35
And Jesus said unto them, I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst.
corruption_summary: A scriptural figure, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses to the emptiness of sin’s provision against the fulness of the Father.
corruption_paragraphs: The husks of the swine are a figure from our Lord’s own parable, and no movement of the present age has troubled itself to redefine them. The dictionary records them that the reader may discern the true worth of all that sin and the world set before the soul, a fodder that has the shape of food but not its substance.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the emptiness of every provision but the LORD’s. He who pictured the prodigal envying the swine their husks is the same who offers Himself as the Bread of life, that he who cometh shall never hunger. The saint tempted by the world’s table may remember the husks, and turn from that which is not bread to the Father’s house, where there is bread enough and to spare.
roots_summary: From the Greek for the “little horn” of the carob, husks name the swine’s fodder of the prodigal’s want.
roots_lines: Husks — Greek keratiōn, the “little horn” or carob pod.
They were the coarse fodder given to swine.
The prodigal longed to fill his belly with them in his want.
No man gave unto him even these in the far country.
They figure the empty provision of sin that does not satisfy.
usage: Like the husks the prodigal craved, the provisions of sin fill the mouth and leave the soul empty and hungry still.
The world spends its labour on that which is not bread, and rises ever unsatisfied from the swine’s table.
The famine of the husks is made, by God’s mercy, the means to turn the wanderer home to the Bread of life.

etymology: From the Greek triches, “hairs,” numbered by the Father, a figure of the minute and exhaustive providence of God over His own.
biblical_def: The hairs of the head are made in Scripture the measure of God’s minute and particular providence over His people, for the Lord Jesus said, But the very hairs of your head are all numbered (Mat 10:30; Luk 12:7). It is a saying of wonderful comfort, set in the midst of His warning that His people should be hated and persecuted; for if the Father marks the fall of a sparrow and has told the hairs of every head, then not the least thing can befall His children but by His knowledge and ordering. Fear ye not therefore, said the Lord, ye are of more value than many sparrows. So great is this keeping that He promised, There shall not an hair of your head perish (Luk 21:18). The same figure was given long before, when the people swore that not one hair of Jonathan’s head should fall to the ground, for he had wrought with God that day (1Sa 14:45). The dictionary marks that the numbering of the hairs is no idle hyperbole but a true word concerning the exhaustive sovereignty of God, who upholds and governs all His creatures and all their actions, down to the smallest. Nothing is too small for His care nor too great for His hand. The believer who knows his every hair is numbered may walk through fire and flood unafraid, assured that not one of them shall perish but by his Father’s will, who counts him of more value than many sparrows.
webster_summary: The numbered hairs of the head, a figure of God’s minute and exhaustive providence over His people.
webster_full: HAIRS OF THE HEAD, named by Christ as all numbered by the Father.
The figure expresses the minute and particular providence of God over His own.
It is set against the fear of persecution, as a ground of comfort.
Christ promised that not an hair of His people’s head should perish.
It witnesses to the exhaustive sovereignty of God over the smallest things.
scriptures: But the very hairs of your head are all numbered.
Luk 12:7
But even the very hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not therefore: ye are of more value than many sparrows.
But there shall not an hair of your head perish.

And the people said unto Saul, Shall Jonathan die, who hath wrought this great salvation in Israel? God forbid: as the LORD liveth, there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground; for he hath wrought with God this day. So the people rescued Jonathan, that he died not.
corruption_summary: A scriptural figure of providence, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses to the minute and exhaustive care of God over His own.
corruption_paragraphs: The numbering of the hairs is a word of our Lord Himself, and no movement of the present age has troubled itself to redefine it. The dictionary records it that the believer may know the comfort it was given to bring, that the Father who marks the sparrow has told the hairs of his head, and orders the least thing that befalls him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the exhaustive providence of God, who governs all His creatures and all their actions down to the smallest. He who numbered the hairs of His people’s heads is the same who has promised that not one of them shall perish but by His will. The saint afraid of what tomorrow may bring may remember that he is of more value than many sparrows, and that his every hair is told before the throne of his Father.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “hairs,” numbered by the Father, the figure names the minute providence of God over His own.
roots_lines: Hairs of the Head — Greek triches, “hairs,” all numbered by God.
Christ gave the saying as comfort against the fear of persecution.
He promised that not an hair of His people’s head should perish.
The people swore that not one hair of Jonathan’s head should fall.
It figures the exhaustive sovereignty of God over the smallest things.
usage: Like the hairs of the head all numbered by the Father, no least thing befalls the believer but by the knowledge and ordering of God.
The saint who walks through fire and flood may be unafraid, for not one hair shall perish but by his Father’s will.
He who counts His children of more value than many sparrows tells the very hairs of their heads.

etymology: From the Hebrew tsur and sela‘, “rock” and “cliff,” titles by which the believer confesses the LORD his strong defence, fortress, and deliverer.
biblical_def: The LORD is my rock is the believer’s confession of God as his strong and unmovable defence, the firm ground beneath him and the high fortress above him. David sang it in the day the LORD delivered him from all his enemies and from the hand of Saul: The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; the God of my rock; in him will I trust (2Sa 22:2-3). He repeated it in the eighteenth psalm, heaping title upon title: The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my strength, in whom I will trust; my buckler, and the horn of my salvation, and my high tower (Psa 18:2). The figure speaks both of refuge and of permanence, for a rock cannot be moved, cannot be shaken, cannot be washed away in the flood. Moses sang of Him: He is the Rock, his work is perfect: for all his ways are judgment; a God of truth and without iniquity, just and right is he (Deu 32:4). And the soul finds its rest there: He only is my rock and my salvation; I shall not be greatly moved (Psa 62:2). The dictionary marks that this Rock is no mere figure of stability but a Person, the LORD Himself, faithful and true; and the New Testament reveals that that Rock was Christ, the sure foundation, the stone the builders refused, become the head of the corner, upon whom the believer builds and is never confounded.
webster_summary: The believer’s confession of the LORD as his unmovable rock, fortress, and deliverer.
webster_full: THE LORD IS MY ROCK, the believer’s confession of God as his strong defence.
David sang it when delivered from all his enemies and from Saul.
The figure joins refuge and permanence, the rock that cannot be moved.
Moses called Him the Rock whose work is perfect and whose ways are judgment.
It witnesses to the LORD, and to Christ the Rock, as the sure foundation of faith.
scriptures: And he said, The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer;
Psa 18:2
The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my strength, in whom I will trust; my buckler, and the horn of my salvation, and my high tower.
Deu 32:4
He is the Rock, his work is perfect: for all his ways are judgment: a God of truth and without iniquity, just and right is he.
Psa 62:2
He only is my rock and my salvation; he is my defence; I shall not be greatly moved.
corruption_summary: A scriptural confession of faith, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses to the LORD as the believer’s unmovable defence.
corruption_paragraphs: The confession that the LORD is my rock is the very language of David and of Moses, and no movement of the present age has troubled itself to redefine it. The dictionary records it that the believer may take upon his own lips the titles of refuge and strength with which the saints of old laid hold upon their God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the unmovable stability of the LORD as the believer’s defence. He who was David’s rock and fortress is the same Rock that followed Israel, even Christ, the sure foundation laid in Zion. The saint shaken by the floods of trouble and the assaults of the enemy may remember that he builds upon a Rock that cannot be moved, and confess with the psalmist, He only is my rock and my salvation; I shall not be greatly moved.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for “rock” and “cliff,” the confession names the LORD the believer’s unmovable defence and deliverer.
roots_lines: The LORD Is My Rock — Hebrew tsur, “rock,” and sela‘, “cliff.”
David sang it in the day of his deliverance from his enemies.
He heaped the titles fortress, deliverer, strength, buckler, and high tower.
Moses called Him the Rock whose work is perfect.
The New Testament reveals that the Rock was Christ.
usage: Like David who sang the LORD his rock, the believer rests upon a defence that cannot be moved by flood or foe.
When the soul is shaken by trouble, it confesses, He only is my rock and my salvation; I shall not be greatly moved.
The Rock that followed Israel was Christ, and he that builds upon Him is never confounded.

etymology: From the Greek aiōn houtos, “this age” or “this present world,” the evil order of things from which Christ delivers, set against ho aiōn ho mellōn, “the age to come.”
biblical_def: This age is the Scripture’s name for the present evil order of the world, fallen under sin and the prince of the power of the air, from which Christ gave Himself to deliver His people. He gave himself for our sins, that he might deliver us from this present evil world, according to the will of God and our Father (Gal 1:4). It is set in plain contrast with the age to come, for God hath set His Son far above all principality and power, not only in this world, but also in that which is to come (Eph 1:21); and the sin against the Holy Ghost shall not be forgiven, neither in this world, neither in the world to come (Mat 12:32). This age has its own wisdom, its own princes that come to nought, its own fashion that passeth away; and the grace of God teaches us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world (Tit 2:12). The dictionary marks that this age is not a neutral span of time but a moral order opposed to God, the kingdom of darkness over which the god of this world holds his usurped dominion. The believer lives in it but is not of it, a pilgrim and a stranger passing through, set free by the cross from its bondage and its doom, and waiting for the age to come, the everlasting kingdom of the Lord Jesus Christ, in which dwelleth righteousness.
webster_summary: The present evil order of the world, from which Christ delivers, set against the age to come.
webster_full: THIS AGE, the present evil order of the world, also called this present world.
Christ gave Himself to deliver His people from this present evil world.
It is set in contrast with the age, or world, to come.
It has its own wisdom, its princes, and its fashion that passeth away.
It witnesses to the believer as a pilgrim, in this age but not of it.
scriptures: Gal 1:4
Who gave himself for our sins, that he might deliver us from this present evil world, according to the will of God and our Father:
Eph 1:21
Far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this world, but also in that which is to come:

And whosoever speaketh a word against the Son of man, it shall be forgiven him: but whosoever speaketh against the Holy Ghost, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this world, neither in the world to come.
Tit 2:12
Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world;
corruption_summary: The spirit of this age presses conformity upon the church, and the love of this present world draws even professors away.
corruption_paragraphs: This age has always had its lovers, and the present hour is no exception. The progressive temper of the times bids the church measure herself by the changing fashions of this present world, to baptize its passing wisdom and conform her doctrine to its shifting standards, until the line between the church and the age is all but rubbed away. Of one such lover the apostle wrote with grief, Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world (2Ti 4:10); and the same draught draws professors still, who would have the name of Christ and the friendship of the age together.

The dictionary answers with the apostle’s charge, Be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind (Rom 12:2). The fashion of this age passeth away, and its wisdom is foolishness with God; the friendship of the world is enmity with God. The recovery is the pilgrim mind that lives in this age as a stranger and not a citizen, set free by the cross from the present evil world, refusing to be squeezed into its mould, and waiting in holiness for the age to come, wherein dwelleth righteousness.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “this present world,” this age names the evil order Christ delivers from, set against the age to come.
roots_lines: This Age — Greek aiōn houtos, “this age” or “this present world.”
It stands against ho aiōn ho mellōn, “the age to come.”
Christ gave Himself to deliver us from this present evil world.
It has its own wisdom and fashion, which passeth away.
The believer lives in it as a pilgrim, not of it.
usage: Like the pilgrim in this present evil age, the believer lives within it as a stranger and not a citizen.
Demas loved this present world and forsook the apostle; the same draught draws professors still.
Be not conformed to this age, but be transformed by the renewing of the mind, waiting for the age to come.

etymology: From the Hebrew musar, “discipline, chastening,” and the Greek epanorthōsis, “a setting straight again,” the reproof and chastening of the LORD and of His Word.
biblical_def: Correction is the reproof and chastening by which the LORD and His Word set the erring straight and bring the wandering back into the way. The Scripture names it among the great profits of the inspired Word: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness, that the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works (2Ti 3:16). It is therefore no harsh or alien thing, but a means of the LORD’s love, and Solomon binds the son not to despise it: My son, despise not the chastening of the LORD; neither be weary of his correction: for whom the LORD loveth he correcteth (Pro 3:11-12). Folly is bound in the heart of a child, but the rod of correction shall drive it far from him (Pro 22:15). The Hebrews take up the same theme, that the LORD chasteneth every son whom He receiveth, and that no chastening for the present seemeth joyous, but grievous; nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby (Heb 12:6-11). The dictionary marks that correction is the LORD’s fatherly dealing, not His wrath, the proof of sonship and not its denial. He who is left uncorrected is no son but a bastard; but the child whom God reproves by His Word and chastens by His hand is made partaker of His holiness, and shall reap the peaceable fruit thereof.
webster_summary: The reproof and chastening of the LORD and His Word, profitable to make the man of God perfect.
webster_full: CORRECTION, the reproof and chastening that sets the erring straight.
It is named a profit of the inspired Word, to perfect the man of God.
Solomon bids the son not to despise the chastening of the LORD.
The rod of correction drives folly far from the heart of a child.
It witnesses to the LORD’s fatherly love, chastening every son He receiveth.
scriptures: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
Pro 3:11
My son, despise not the chastening of the LORD; neither be weary of his correction:
Foolishness is bound in the heart of a child; but the rod of correction shall drive it far from him.
Heb 12:6
For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth.
corruption_summary: The present age rejects all correction and discipline as harmful, and would strip from the Word and the family the LORD’s loving chastening.
corruption_paragraphs: The spirit of the age has set itself against correction in every form, naming all reproof and discipline as harmful, and bidding men affirm what is in them rather than reprove it. The Word that is profitable for reproof and correction is recast as too sharp for tender hearts; the rod that drives folly from a child is forbidden; the chastening hand of the heavenly Father is mistaken for cruelty. So a whole generation is taught to despise the very thing the Scripture calls the proof of a Father’s love, and to flee from the discipline that alone can make the wandering wise.

The dictionary answers in the plain words of Scripture, not in the borrowed speech of the age. Correction is the LORD’s fatherly dealing with His own; whom He loveth He chasteneth, and scourgeth every son He receiveth, and the child left uncorrected is no true son but a bastard. No chastening seemeth joyous for the present, but grievous; yet afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness to them that are exercised thereby. The recovery is to despise not the chastening of the LORD, to receive His reproof as love and not as cruelty, and to submit son and self alike to the correcting Word that the man of God may be perfect.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for “chastening” and the Greek for “a setting straight,” correction names the LORD’s loving reproof of His own.
roots_lines: Correction — Hebrew musar, “discipline, chastening.”
The Greek epanorthōsis means “a setting straight again.”
All Scripture is profitable for reproof and for correction.
The rod of correction drives folly from the heart of a child.
The LORD chasteneth every son whom He receiveth, in love.
usage: Like the chastening that proves a father’s love, the LORD’s correction is the mark of sonship and not its denial.
The believer is bid not to despise the chastening of the LORD, but to receive His reproof as the dealing of love.
No correction seemeth joyous for the present, yet afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness.
